title: MOSFETs
description: NMOS and PMOS transistors: regions of operation, the square law, bias points and switching.

study.title: The NMOS transistor
study.body: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET has n-type source and drain regions in a p-type body. The gate is insulated by a thin oxide, so the gate current is zero. When $v_{GS}$ exceeds the **threshold voltage** $V_{to}$, electrons gather under the gate and form an n-type channel: $i_D$ flows into the drain and out of the source. The designer sets the channel width $W$ and length $L$.

study.title: Regions of an NMOS
study.body:
- **Cutoff:** $v_{GS} \le V_{to}$: $i_D = 0$.
- **Triode:** $v_{GS} \ge V_{to}$ and $0 \le v_{DS} \le v_{GS} - V_{to}$: $i_D = K\left[2(v_{GS} - V_{to})v_{DS} - v_{DS}^2\right]$.
- **Saturation:** $v_{GS} \ge V_{to}$ and $v_{DS} \ge v_{GS} - V_{to}$: $i_D = K(v_{GS} - V_{to})^2$.
The device constant depends on the geometry and on the process parameter $KP$ (typically 50 µA/V² for NMOS):

study.title: Triode–saturation boundary
study.body:
The boundary is $v_{DS} = v_{GS} - V_{to}$, which is the same as $v_{GD} = V_{to}$: the channel just pinches off at the drain end. In the $i_D$–$v_{DS}$ plane it is the parabola $i_D = Kv_{DS}^2$.
Quick test: **triode** if both $v_{GS}$ and $v_{GD}$ exceed $V_{to}$; **saturation** if $v_{GS}$ exceeds $V_{to}$ but $v_{GD}$ does not.

study.title: PMOS transistors
study.body:
Swap n and p: the symbol is drawn with the source on top and $i_D$ is referenced **out of** the drain, so it is positive. $V_{to}$ is negative (typically −1 V) and $KP$ is about 25 µA/V².
- **Cutoff:** $v_{GS} \ge V_{to}$
- **Triode:** $v_{GS} \le V_{to}$ and $0 \ge v_{DS} \ge v_{GS} - V_{to}$
- **Saturation:** $v_{GS} \le V_{to}$ and $v_{DS} \le v_{GS} - V_{to}$
The current equations are the same as for NMOS.

study.title: Finding the Q point
study.body: In the fixed- plus self-bias circuit no gate current flows, so $V_G = V_{DD}R_2/(R_1+R_2)$. Gate loop: $V_G = V_{GS} + R_S I_D$. Assume saturation, $I_D = K(V_{GS} - V_{to})^2$, solve the quadratic and keep the root with $V_{GS} > V_{to}$. Then $V_{DS} = V_{DD} - (R_D + R_S)I_D$; check $V_{DS} \ge V_{GS} - V_{to}$. With $R_S = 0$ simply $V_{GS} = V_G$.

study.title: The MOSFET as a switch
study.body: Gate low ($v_{GS} = 0 < V_{to}$): cutoff, an open switch, so $v_{DS} = V_{DD}$. Gate high: the channel conducts and with a load resistor the transistor ends up in the triode region with a small $v_{DS}$. For small $v_{DS}$, $i_D \approx 2K(v_{GS} - V_{to})v_{DS}$, so the switch behaves like a resistance:

steps.title: Drain, gate, source
steps.body: A MOSFET has a **drain** (D), **gate** (G) and **source** (S). The gate sits on a thin insulating oxide, so no gate current flows. The gate-to-source voltage $v_{GS}$ controls how much current flows from drain to source.

steps.prompt: In DC analysis, the gate current of a MOSFET can be taken as zero.
steps.explanation: The gate is insulated from the channel by silicon dioxide, so practically no current flows into it. That's why a gate voltage divider can be analyzed as an unloaded divider.

steps.prompt: What forms the conducting channel in an NMOS transistor?
options: Electrons attracted under the gate by a positive $v_{GS}$ above $V_{to}$
Holes injected through the gate oxide
Current flowing from the gate into the body
steps.explanation: A positive gate voltage pushes holes away from the p-type region under the gate and attracts electrons. Once $v_{GS} > V_{to}$ there are enough electrons to form an n-type channel between drain and source.

steps.title: Three regions
steps.body:
- **Cutoff** ($v_{GS} \le V_{to}$): no channel, $i_D = 0$.
- **Triode** ($v_{DS} < v_{GS} - V_{to}$): the channel acts like a voltage-controlled resistor.
- **Saturation** ($v_{DS} \ge v_{GS} - V_{to}$): the channel is pinched off at the drain and $i_D$ no longer depends on $v_{DS}$.

steps.prompt: Match each NMOS region with its conditions
steps.explanation: First compare $v_{GS}$ with $V_{to}$ (on or off). If on, compare $v_{DS}$ with the overdrive $v_{GS} - V_{to}$: below it is triode, above it is saturation.

steps.prompt: An NMOS with $V_{to}$ = {{Vto}} V operates at $v_{GS}$ = {{vGS}} V and $v_{DS}$ = {{vDS}} V. In which region is it?
steps.explanation: $v_{GS}$ = {{vGS}} V > $V_{to}$, so the transistor is on. The boundary is $v_{GS} - V_{to}$ = {{ov}} V, and $v_{DS}$ = {{vDS}} V is larger, so it operates in **saturation**.

steps.title: The square law
steps.body:
In saturation the drain current depends only on the overdrive $v_{GS} - V_{to}$:
$$i_D = K(v_{GS} - V_{to})^2$$
The device constant $K$ grows with the width-to-length ratio of the channel.

steps.prompt: An NMOS has $W$ = {{W}} µm, $L$ = {{L}} µm and $KP$ = {{KP}} µA/V². Find the device constant $K$.
steps.explanation: $K = \frac{W}{L}\cdot\frac{KP}{2} = \frac{ {{W}} }{ {{L}} }\times\frac{ {{KP}}\ \mu\text{A/V}^2}{2}$ = {{K|A/V²}}.

steps.prompt: An NMOS with $K$ = {{K|A/V²}} and $V_{to}$ = {{Vto}} V is in saturation with $v_{GS}$ = {{vGS}} V. Find $i_D$.
steps.explanation:
$i_D = K(v_{GS} - V_{to})^2 = {{K}}\times({{vGS}} - {{Vto}})^2$ = {{K*ov^2|A}}.
Note the square: doubling the overdrive quadruples the current.

steps.prompt: An NMOS with $V_{to}$ = {{Vto}} V has $v_{GS}$ = {{vGS}} V and $v_{DS}$ = {{vDS}} V. In which region does it operate?
steps.explanation: $v_{GS} > V_{to}$, so it is on. $v_{GS} - V_{to}$ = {{ov}} V, and $v_{DS}$ = {{vDS}} V is **smaller**, so it is in the **triode** region. Equivalently $v_{GD}$ = {{vGS-vDS}} V is still above $V_{to}$: the channel is not pinched off.

steps.prompt: An NMOS with $K$ = {{K|A/V²}} and $V_{to}$ = {{Vto}} V operates at $v_{GS}$ = {{vGS}} V and $v_{DS}$ = {{vDS}} V (triode region). Find $i_D$.
steps.explanation:
Triode: $i_D = K\left[2(v_{GS} - V_{to})v_{DS} - v_{DS}^2\right] = {{K}}\left[2\times{{ov}}\times{{vDS}} - {{vDS}}^2\right]$ = {{K*(2*ov*vDS - vDS^2)|A}}.
The saturation formula would wrongly give {{K*ov^2|A}}.

steps.prompt: An NMOS with $V_{to}$ = {{Vto}} V has $v_{GS}$ = {{vGS}} V. What is the smallest $v_{DS}$ for which it is in saturation?
steps.explanation: Saturation requires $v_{DS} \ge v_{GS} - V_{to}$ = {{vGS}} − {{Vto}} = {{vGS-Vto|V}}. At that point $v_{GD} = V_{to}$ and the channel just pinches off at the drain.

steps.prompt: An NMOS with $V_{to}$ = {{Vto}} V has $v_{GS}$ = {{vGS}} V and $v_{DS}$ = {{vDS}} V. What is $i_D$?
steps.explanation: $v_{GS}$ = {{vGS}} V is below the threshold {{Vto}} V, so no channel forms: cutoff, $i_D = 0$, however large $v_{DS}$ is. (Plugging into the square law would give a nonzero value, which is wrong.)

steps.prompt: Find the drain current $I_D$. The NMOS has $K$ = {{K|A/V²}} and $V_{to}$ = 1.5 V.
steps.explanation:
No gate current, so the divider is unloaded: $V_G = {{VDD}}\times\frac{1\text{ M}}{ {{R1/1000000}}\text{ M} + 1\text{ M} }$ = {{VG|V}} $= V_{GS}$ (source grounded).
Assume saturation: $I_D = K(V_{GS} - V_{to})^2 = {{K}}\times({{VG}} - 1.5)^2$ = {{ID|A}}.
Check: $V_{DS} = V_{DD} - R_D I_D$ = {{VDS|V}} ≥ $V_{GS} - V_{to}$ = {{VG-1.5|V}} ✓.

steps.prompt: Same circuit type: $V_{DD}$ = {{VDD|V}}, $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = 1 MΩ, $R_D$ = {{RD|Ω}}, source grounded, $K$ = {{K|A/V²}}, $V_{to}$ = 1.5 V. Find $V_{DS}$ at the Q point.
steps.explanation:
$V_{GS} = V_G = {{VDD}}\times\frac{1}{ {{R1/1000000}} + 1}$ = {{VG|V}}.
$I_D = K(V_{GS} - V_{to})^2$ = {{ID|A}} (assuming saturation).
$V_{DS} = V_{DD} - R_D I_D = {{VDD}} - {{RD}}\times{{ID}}$ = {{VDS|V}}, which is ≥ {{VG-1.5|V}}, so saturation is confirmed.

steps.prompt: A PMOS with $V_{to}$ = −1 V operating at $v_{GS}$ = −3 V and $v_{DS}$ = −1 V is in saturation.
steps.explanation: $v_{GS} = -3 \le V_{to} = -1$, so it is on. Saturation needs $v_{DS} \le v_{GS} - V_{to} = -3 - (-1) = -2$ V. Here $v_{DS} = -1$ V is **above** −2 V, so it is in the **triode** region. For PMOS all the inequalities flip.

steps.prompt: A PMOS has $K$ = {{K|A/V²}} and $V_{to}$ = {{Vto}} V. It operates at $v_{GS}$ = {{vGS}} V and $v_{DS}$ = {{vDS}} V. Find $i_D$ (referenced out of the drain).
steps.explanation:
On: $v_{GS}$ = {{vGS}} V ≤ $V_{to}$. Saturation: $v_{DS}$ = {{vDS}} V ≤ $v_{GS} - V_{to}$ = {{vGS-Vto}} V ✓.
$i_D = K(v_{GS} - V_{to})^2 = {{K}}\times({{vGS-Vto}})^2$ = {{K*(vGS-Vto)^2|A}}, positive out of the drain.

steps.prompt: Tap the **two** nodes whose voltage difference is $v_{GS}$.
steps.explanation:
$v_{GS}$ is the gate voltage measured from the **source**: $v_{GS} = v_G - v_S$.
- Node 1 (the $R_1$–$R_2$ divider) drives the gate.
- Node 3 is the source; it sits $I_D R_S$ above ground, so $v_{GS}$ is **not** simply $v_G$.
Node 2 is the drain and node 4 the supply. In this self-biased circuit $V_G = V_{GS} + I_D R_S$.

steps.prompt: In a fixed- plus self-bias circuit the gate divider gives $V_G$ = {{VG|V}}; the source resistor is $R_S$ = {{RS|Ω}}. The NMOS has $K$ = {{K|A/V²}} and $V_{to}$ = {{Vto}} V. Assuming saturation, find $I_D$.
steps.explanation:
Gate loop: $V_G = V_{GS} + R_S I_D$ with $I_D = K x^2$, $x = V_{GS} - V_{to}$:
$R_S K x^2 + x - (V_G - V_{to}) = 0$, i.e. ${{a}}x^2 + x - {{VG-Vto}} = 0$.
Positive root: $x = \frac{-1 + \sqrt{1 + 4({{a}})({{VG-Vto}})}}{2({{a}})}$ = {{x}} V, so $V_{GS}$ = {{x+Vto|V}}.
$I_D = Kx^2$ = {{ID|A}}. Check: $V_{GS} + R_S I_D$ = {{x+Vto+RS*ID}} V = $V_G$ ✓.

steps.prompt: A fixed- plus self-bias circuit has $V_{DD}$ = {{VDD|V}}, $V_G$ = {{VG|V}}, $R_S$ = {{RS|Ω}}, $R_D$ = {{RD|Ω}}; the NMOS has $K$ = 1 mA/V², $V_{to}$ = 1 V. Find $V_{DS}$.
steps.explanation:
Solve the gate loop with $x = V_{GS} - V_{to}$: $R_SKx^2 + x - (V_G - V_{to}) = 0$ gives $x$ = {{x}} V and $I_D = Kx^2$ = {{ID|A}}.
Drain loop: $V_{DS} = V_{DD} - (R_D + R_S)I_D = {{VDD}} - ({{RD}} + {{RS}})\times{{ID}}$ = {{VDS|V}}.
Check saturation: {{VDS}} V ≥ $V_{GS} - V_{to}$ = {{x}} V ✓.

steps.prompt: Solving $V_G = V_{GS} + R_S K(V_{GS} - V_{to})^2$ gives two roots for $V_{GS}$. Which one is the real operating point?
options: Either root, they give the same $I_D$
steps.explanation: The square law $K(V_{GS} - V_{to})^2$ is only valid for $V_{GS} > V_{to}$; for lower $V_{GS}$ the transistor is cut off and $I_D = 0$. The other root is extraneous: it lies on the mirrored half of the parabola.

steps.prompt: An NMOS switch with $K$ = {{K|A/V²}} and $V_{to}$ = {{Vto}} V is driven with $v_{GS}$ = {{VGS}} V. Estimate its on-resistance for small $v_{DS}$.
steps.explanation:
For small $v_{DS}$ the $v_{DS}^2$ term in the triode equation is negligible: $i_D \approx 2K(v_{GS} - V_{to})v_{DS}$. So
$r_{DS} = \frac{1}{2K(v_{GS} - V_{to})} = \frac{1}{2\times{{K}}\times{{VGS-Vto}} }$ = {{1/(2*K*(VGS-Vto))|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: In the switch circuit, $v_{in} = V_{DD}$ = {{VDD|V}}, $R_D$ = {{RD|Ω}}, $K$ = {{K|A/V²}}, $V_{to}$ = 1 V. Model the on transistor by its small-$v_{DS}$ resistance and find $v_{DS}$.
steps.explanation:
$r_{DS} = \frac{1}{2K(V_{DD} - V_{to})} = \frac{1}{2\times{{K}}\times{{VDD-1}} }$ = {{r|Ω}}.
Divider: $v_{DS} = V_{DD}\frac{r_{DS}}{R_D + r_{DS}}$ = {{vDS|V}}. This is far below $v_{GS} - V_{to}$, so the triode assumption holds: the switch is nearly closed.

steps.prompt: In the same switch circuit ($V_{DD}$ = {{VDD|V}}, $R_D$ = {{RD|Ω}}, $V_{to}$ = 1 V), the input is $v_{in}$ = 0 V. What is $v_{DS}$?
steps.explanation: $v_{GS} = 0 < V_{to}$: cutoff, $i_D = 0$. With no current there is no drop across $R_D$, so the drain sits at $V_{DD}$: $v_{DS}$ = {{VDD|V}}. The switch is open.

steps.prompt: A designer needs an NMOS with $K$ = {{K|A/V²}} in a process with $KP$ = 50 µA/V². What width-to-length ratio $W/L$ is required?
steps.explanation: $K = \frac{W}{L}\cdot\frac{KP}{2}$, so $\frac{W}{L} = \frac{2K}{KP} = \frac{2\times{{K}}}{50\times10^{-6}}$ = {{2*K/50e-6}}.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for finding the Q point of a fixed- plus self-bias NMOS circuit in order
items: Find $V_G$ from the gate divider (no gate current)
Solve with $V_G = V_{GS} + R_S I_D$; keep the root with $V_{GS} > V_{to}$
steps.explanation: The gate side gives $V_G$ directly because $I_G = 0$. Combining the bias line with the square law yields $I_D$; the drain loop then gives $V_{DS}$, and the final check confirms the saturation assumption.

steps.prompt: CMOS inverter. Tap every node that is connected to the **source** terminal of a transistor.
steps.explanation:
Each transistor has its source on the **supply side**:
- The PMOS (top) has its source at the top, on $V_{DD}$ (node 1). It turns on when its gate is well **below** $V_{DD}$.
- The NMOS (bottom) has its source at the bottom, on ground (node 3).
The two drains meet at the output (node 2), and the gates are joined at the input (node 4).

steps.prompt: The graph shows the output characteristics of an NMOS with $V_{to}$ = {{Vto|V}}. Find the device constant $K$.
steps.explanation: In saturation (the flat part of each curve) $i_D = K(v_{GS} - V_{to})^2$. The top curve has $v_{GS} - V_{to}$ = 4 V and levels off at {{16*K|A}}, so $K$ = {{16*K|A}} / (4 V)² = {{K*1000||3}} mA/V². The other curves give the same: {{9*K|A}} / (3 V)² and {{4*K|A}} / (2 V)².

steps.prompt: The graph shows the output characteristics of an NMOS with $V_{to}$ = {{Vto|V}}. In which region does it operate at point P?
steps.explanation: On each curve the region boundary is at $v_{DS} = v_{GS} - V_{to}$, where the rising (triode) part bends into the flat (saturation) part. P lies on the curve for $v_{GS}$ = {{Vto+c|V}}, whose boundary is at $v_{DS}$ = {{c|V}}; P is at $v_{DS}$ ≈ {{px||2}} V. Left of the boundary means triode, right of it saturation.

steps.prompt: This NMOS ($V_{to}$ = {{Vto|V}}) is biased at $v_{GS}$ = {{Vto+c|V}}. The curves are for $v_{GS}$ = {{Vto+2|V}}, {{Vto+3|V}} and {{Vto+4|V}} (bottom to top); the orange line is the load line of the drain circuit.
steps.explanation: The Q point is where the load line crosses the curve for $v_{GS}$ = {{Vto+c|V}}: $i_D$ ≈ {{iQ|A}} and $v_{DS}$ ≈ {{vQ|V}}. Check: $v_{DS} = V_{DD} - R_Di_D$ = {{VDD|V}} − {{RD|Ω}} × {{iQ|A}} = {{vQ|V}}. Since $v_{DS}$ > $v_{GS} - V_{to}$ = {{c|V}}, the transistor is in saturation, on the flat part of the curve.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the transfer characteristic $i_D$ versus $v_{GS}$ of an NMOS in saturation. Read the threshold voltage $V_{to}$.
steps.explanation: Below the threshold there is no channel and $i_D$ = 0. The curve leaves the axis at $v_{GS}$ ≈ {{Vto|V}}, so $V_{to}$ ≈ {{Vto|V}}. (A parabola starts off very flat, so the visible rise begins a little to the right of $V_{to}$.) Above it the current grows with the square of the overdrive: $i_D = K(v_{GS} - V_{to})^2$, e.g. {{K|A}} × (1 V)² = {{K|A}} at $v_{GS}$ = {{Vto+1|V}}.

steps.prompt: Which graph shows $i_D$ versus $v_{DS}$ of an NMOS for one fixed $v_{GS} > V_{to}$?
steps.explanation: For small $v_{DS}$ (triode) the channel acts like a resistor and $i_D$ rises almost linearly. Once $v_{DS}$ exceeds $v_{GS} - V_{to}$ the channel pinches off at the drain and $i_D = K(v_{GS} - V_{to})^2$ stays constant (saturation): the curve flattens. A straight line is a resistor; an exponential is a diode.
